summary: 2 Timothy 3 (17 verses) continues the story of endurance. Starting with 'But know this: that in the last days, grievous times will come.', it moves through themes of endurance, Scripture and calls readers toward Scripture.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows endurance lived out in paul near death. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: But know this: that in the last days, grievous times will come.
But they will proceed no further. For their folly will be evident to all men, as theirs also came to be.
that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.

questions.question: What is happening in 2 Timothy 3?
questions.answer: In 17 verses, this chapter 2 timothy 3 (17 verses) continues the story of endurance. starting with 'but know this: that in the last days, grievous times will come.', it moves through themes of endurance, scripture and calls readers toward scripture. The setting is paul near death, written to timothy. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote 2 Timothy and why 3 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally paul, addressed to timothy around ad 64-67 final days. This chapter fits the book's purpose as pastoral exhortation — its themes of endurance, Scripture build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'righteousness' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Being in right standing, doing what is right. In this chapter, it appears in context of endurance. For a first-time reader: think of it as being in right standing, doing what is right, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through endurance and Scripture, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 11 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'persecutions, and sufferings—those things that happened to me at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra. I endured those persecutions. The Lord delivered me out of them all....' In plain terms: it is making a key point about endurance. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?

glossary.def: Being in right standing, doing what is right
